advances: Classifies exact midpoint stationarity for all admissible finite tables without a parity-balance assumption. Proves an absolute linear squared-Hellinger rigidity bound for one-dimensional log-concave interval tables and, by tensorization, a dimension-independent off-diagonal bound for their products and affine unimodular images. The quantitative conclusion is restricted to this product class and does not establish small-gain stability for general coupled tables.

proof:
For any probability table, retain the canonical quantity \(R_j=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^n}p_{j+v}p_{j-v}\). The conditioning identities of accepted fact ab57fac07c0d3160(i) give \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}_j=R_j/q\), \(q\ge2^{-n}\), and \(a(p)=1-q^{-1}\sum_jp_j^2\). The same identities for any countably supported probability table follow directly: the map \((j,v)\mapsto(j+v,j-v)\) is a bijection onto ordered same-parity endpoint pairs, so summing their nonnegative probabilities gives \(\sum_jR_j=q\); Cauchy-Schwarz on the parity masses gives the lower bound for \(q\). We will use this countable version for a limiting one-dimensional table.

Two elementary distance bounds used below are \(d_{\mathrm H}^2(u,v)\le\operatorname{TV}(u,v)\le\sqrt{2d_{\mathrm H}^2(u,v)}\). The first follows termwise from \((\sqrt{s}-\sqrt{t})^2\le|s-t|\). For the second, factor \(|u_z-v_z|=|\sqrt{u_z}-\sqrt{v_z}|(\sqrt{u_z}+\sqrt{v_z})\), apply Cauchy-Schwarz, and use \(\sum_z(\sqrt{u_z}+\sqrt{v_z})^2\le4\).

A one-dimensional table in item 2 has the required global extension. On its positive real interval, interpolate \(\log r_k\) affinely between adjacent integers. The inequalities \(r_k^2\ge r_{k-1}r_{k+1}\) say exactly that the interpolation slopes are nonincreasing, so the interpolated logarithm is concave. Exponentiate on the closed interval and set the extension to zero outside it. If the support is a singleton, assign its mass at that point and zero elsewhere. In both cases the extension is finite-valued, is globally log-concave, and agrees at every integer, including every zero. In particular, within the positive support all integer chord inequalities for \(\log r\) hold. Such a table is unimodal, and after translating a mode to zero it is nonincreasing to the right and nondecreasing to the left.

For item 1, suppose \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}=p\). The stationarity equation \(qp_j=R_j\ge p_j^2\) implies \(p_j\le q\) for every \(j\in A\). If \(z\) is a vertex of \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\), the only supported pair with midpoint \(z\) is \((z,z)\): an extreme point cannot be the midpoint of two distinct points of this convex hull. Hence \(qp_z=p_z^2\), giving \(p_z=q\) at every vertex. Every point of \(A\) is a convex combination of these finitely many vertices. Applying global log-concavity to the normalized extension \(f/W\), with repeated two-point interpolation if necessary, gives \(p_j\ge q\) throughout \(A\). Consequently every positive atom equals \(q\). Now \(R_j=qp_j=p_j^2\), so all its nonzero-displacement summands vanish. A distinct positive same-parity pair would have a positive integer midpoint, by global log-concavity, and would contribute a positive nonzero-displacement summand there. Thus there is at most one positive site in each parity class, and \(a(p)=0\).

Conversely, suppose \(p\) is uniform on a support of size \(s\) having at most one point per parity class. Then \(q=1/s\), and every supported same-parity pair is diagonal. Therefore \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}_j=p_j^2/q=p_j\) at positive sites and is zero elsewhere. This proves item 1, also for lower-dimensional supports and for a singleton.

We first prove a local one-dimensional estimate. Let \(I=[L,R]\cap\mathbb Z\), with \(R-L\in\{0,1\}\), let \(r_L,r_R\ge1/3\), and suppose \(t=r(I^c)\le1/1000\). For a singleton these two endpoint inequalities are the same inequality. Put \(u_-=r_{L-1}\) and \(u_+=r_{R+1}\), assigning zero to missing atoms. The monotonicity of ratios of a log-concave sequence shows that farther left-tail ratios are at most \(u_-/r_L\), and farther right-tail ratios are at most \(u_+/r_R\). If an adjacent mass is zero, the corresponding entire tail is zero because the positive support is an interval. Otherwise summing the two geometric bounds yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
B&:=\sum_{k\le L-2}r_k+\sum_{k\ge R+2}r_k\\
&\le\frac{u_-^2}{r_L-u_-}+\frac{u_+^2}{r_R-u_+}
\le\frac{u_-^2+u_+^2}{1/3-t}
\le4t^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

All denominators are positive; the last inequality uses \(u_-+u_+\le t\) and \((1/3-t)^{-1}<4\).

Consider a same-parity ordered pair whose midpoint lies outside \(I\). Either both endpoints are outside \(I\), or an exterior endpoint lies in the far tail counted by \(B\). To check the latter assertion, if \(I\) is a singleton, its two adjacent exterior sites have opposite parity to it. If \(I\) has two sites, pairing either adjacent exterior site with the unique same-parity site of \(I\) gives a midpoint in \(I\). Thus, with \(s=r^{\mathrm{mid}}(I^c)\) and \(q(r)\ge1/2\),

\[
s\le\frac{t^2+2B}{q(r)}\le18t^2\le t/16.
\]

Cauchy-Schwarz restricted to \(I^c\) now gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\mathrm H}^2(r,r^{\mathrm{mid}})
&\ge\frac12\sum_{k\in I^c}(\sqrt{r_k}-\sqrt{r^{\mathrm{mid}}_k})^2\\
&\ge\frac12(\sqrt t-\sqrt s)^2
\ge\frac{9t}{32}\ge\frac t4.
\end{aligned}
\]

Two distinct sites in \(I\) cannot have equal parity. Hence every off-diagonal same-parity pair has at least one endpoint outside \(I\), giving \(a(r)\le2t/q(r)\le4t\). We have proved the local estimate \(d_{\mathrm H}^2(r,r^{\mathrm{mid}})\ge a(r)/16\). It includes \(t=0\), when \(a(r)=0\).

Next we prove the compactness assertion needed to apply this estimate: if \(r^{(m)}\) are tables in item 2 and \(d_{\mathrm H}^2(r^{(m)},(r^{(m)})^{\mathrm{mid}})\to0\), then after translations and a subsequence they converge in \(\ell^1\) to a point mass or to the uniform law on two adjacent integers. Integer translations preserve the midpoint operation and both distances, so translate a mode of each table to zero. Set \(M_m=r^{(m)}_0=\max_k r^{(m)}_k\), and pass to a subsequence for which \(M_m\to M\in[0,1]\).

Suppose first that \(M>0\). Choose \(m_0>0\) with \(M_m\ge m_0\) for all sufficiently large \(m\), and an integer \(L_0\ge2/m_0\). Unimodality and normalization give \(r^{(m)}_{\pm L_0}\le1/(L_0+1)\le M_m/2\). Indeed, each of the \(L_0+1\) sites between zero and either endpoint has mass at least that endpoint's mass. Concavity of \(\log r^{(m)}\), applied to the chord from zero to \(k\), gives, for \(|k|\ge L_0\),

\[
r^{(m)}_k
\le M_m\left(\frac{r^{(m)}_{\operatorname{sgn}(k)L_0}}{M_m}\right)^{|k|/L_0}
\le2^{-|k|/L_0}.
\]

If the intermediate endpoint has zero mass, the farther tail is zero, so the same bound holds. The bound is summable uniformly in \(m\); it also bounds fourth moments uniformly by \(L_0^4+2\sum_{k\ge L_0}k^4 2^{-k/L_0}<\infty\). Choose a diagonal subsequence converging at every integer. The summable tail bound implies that the limit \(r\) has total mass one and that convergence is in \(\ell^1\). It also gives \(r_0=M>0\). Passing to the integer chord inequalities shows that the positive support of \(r\) is an interval and that its logarithm is concave there: positive endpoint limits force every intermediate lattice value to stay positive with the requisite geometric lower bound.

The midpoint operation is continuous in \(\ell^1\), including for countably supported probability tables on \(\mathbb Z\). To see this, for such tables \(u,v\), the independent-pair laws differ in \(\ell^1\) by at most \(2\|u-v\|_1\), using \(u\otimes u-v\otimes v=(u-v)\otimes u+v\otimes(u-v)\). Restricting to equal parity and pushing forward to the midpoint cannot increase this norm. Thus \(\|R(u)-R(v)\|_1\le2\|u-v\|_1\), where \(R(u)_j=\sum_tu_{j+t}u_{j-t}\) is the canonical \(R_j\) evaluated at \(u\). Also \(|q(u)-q(v)|\le\|R(u)-R(v)\|_1\), and normalization with \(q(u),q(v)\ge1/2\) gives

\[
\|u^{\mathrm{mid}}-v^{\mathrm{mid}}\|_1
\le\frac{\|R(u)-R(v)\|_1+|q(u)-q(v)|}{q(u)}
\le8\|u-v\|_1.
\]

The assumed Hellinger convergence implies \(\|r^{(m)}-(r^{(m)})^{\mathrm{mid}}\|_1\to0\). Combining these two facts proves \(r^{\mathrm{mid}}=r\).

We must exclude infinite support for this limiting stationary sequence. The same integer \(L_0\) satisfies \(r_{\pm L_0}\le r_0/2\). Let \(\theta=2^{-1/L_0}<1\). Monotonicity of successive log-concave ratios gives \(r_{k+1}\le\theta r_k\) for \(k\ge L_0\) and \(r_{k-1}\le\theta r_k\) for \(k\le-L_0\). For example, if \(r_{L_0}>0\), every ratio beyond \(L_0\) is at most the geometric mean \((r_{L_0}/r_0)^{1/L_0}\le\theta\) of the first \(L_0\) rightward ratios. If \(r_{L_0}=0\), the right tail is zero. The left side is identical with its orientation reversed.

Fix \(j\) with \(r_j>0\) and put \(v_0=|j|+L_0\). Midpoint log-concavity gives \(r_{j+v}r_{j-v}\le r_j^2\) for every integer \(v\). Once \(v\ge v_0\), both endpoints lie in the outward tails just bounded, and increasing \(v\) by one multiplies their product by at most \(\theta^2\). Splitting the displacement sum into \(|v|<v_0\) and the two geometric tails therefore gives the sufficient bound

\[
R_j(r)
\le\left(2(|j|+L_0)+1+\frac{2}{1-\theta^2}\right)r_j^2.
\]

If the support were infinite, it would contain positive sites with \(|j|\to\infty\). The inherited bound \(r_j\le2^{-|j|/L_0}\) would then force \(R_j(r)/r_j\to0\). Stationarity instead requires \(R_j(r)/r_j=q(r)\ge1/2\) at every such site. This contradiction makes the support finite. The extension constructed above and item 1 now apply to \(r\). A positive integer interval with at most one site per parity has size one or two, and in the latter case its sites are adjacent. Stationarity makes its masses uniform. This proves the compactness assertion in the case \(M>0\).

It remains to exclude \(M_m\to0\). Let \(X_m\) have table \(r^{(m)}\), set \(Z_m=M_mX_m\), and denote its law by \(\nu_m\). Put \(\ell_m=\lceil2/M_m\rceil\). The preceding unimodality and chord argument, now with this varying length, gives \(r^{(m)}_k\le M_m2^{-|k|/\ell_m}\) for \(|k|\ge\ell_m\), while \(M_m\ell_m\le3\). Take the fixed constants \(c=(\log2)/3\) and \(C_{\mathrm{tail}}=4/(1-e^{-c})\). Outside this interval, \(2^{-|k|/\ell_m}\le e^{-cM_m|k|}\). Inside it, \(e^{-cM_m|k|}\ge1/2\) and \(r^{(m)}_k\le M_m\). Consequently \(r^{(m)}_k\le2M_m e^{-cM_m|k|}\) at every site. Summing the two geometric tails and using \(1-e^{-cM_m}\ge(1-e^{-c})M_m\), which follows by concavity on \(0\le M_m\le1\), gives for every \(t\ge0\)

\[
\nu_m\{|z|>t\}
\le\frac{4M_m}{1-e^{-cM_m}}e^{-ct}
\le C_{\mathrm{tail}}e^{-ct}.
\]

These are explicit uniform exponential tails. In particular, for every integer \(s\ge1\), the layer-cake identity gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E|Z_m|^s
&\le C_{\mathrm{tail}}\,\frac{s!}{c^s},\\
\mathbb E\bigl[|Z_m|^s\mathbf1_{\{|Z_m|>T\}}\bigr]
&\le C_{\mathrm{tail}}\left(T^se^{-cT}
 +s\int_T^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-ct}\,dt\right)\longrightarrow0
\end{aligned}
\]

uniformly in \(m\) as \(T\to\infty\). The conditional endpoint law under \(\Gamma_m:=\Gamma_{r^{(m)}}\) has density \(\pi_{k\bmod2}(r^{(m)})/q(r^{(m)})\le2\) relative to \(r^{(m)}\). Thus its rescaled tails and moments satisfy the same bounds with an additional factor two. If the rescaled midpoint has absolute value greater than \(t\), at least one rescaled endpoint does, so its tail satisfies the displayed exponential bound with an additional factor four. These estimates supply uniform fourth moments and uniform integrability of second moments for the original, conditioned endpoint, and midpoint laws independently of any distance estimate.

The tail bound makes \((\nu_m)\) tight. Passing to a weakly convergent subsequence gives a probability law \(\nu\); equivalently, one may select the distribution functions on rational arguments and use the same tightness bound to exclude loss of mass at infinity. Each atom of \(\nu_m\) has mass at most \(M_m\), and its grid has spacing \(M_m\). Every open interval therefore satisfies \(\nu_m((a,b))\le b-a+M_m\). The open-set inequality for weak convergence yields \(\nu((a,b))\le b-a\). Shrinking an interval around any point shows that \(\nu\) is atomless, so it is not concentrated at a single point. The explicit moment bounds, applied first to bounded continuous truncations of \(|z|^2\), give \(\int z^2\,d\nu(z)\le2C_{\mathrm{tail}}/c^2<\infty\). Hence \(\nu\) has finite strictly positive variance. The displayed uniform tail-moment estimate would also justify first and second moment convergence by truncation; no such convergence is being inferred from total variation.

We now verify convergence under parity conditioning. For any finitely supported unimodal probability sequence with maximum \(M_m\), telescoping on both sides of its modes gives \(\sum_k|r^{(m)}_{k+1}-r^{(m)}_k|=2M_m\). In particular, if \(\pi_{m,b}=\pi_b(r^{(m)})\), then

\[
|\pi_{m,0}-\pi_{m,1}|
\le\sum_k|r^{(m)}_{2k}-r^{(m)}_{2k+1}|
\le2M_m.
\]

For large \(m\), \(M_m\le1/4\), so each parity mass is at least \(1/4\). After moving every odd site one lattice unit left, the two parity-conditioned tables have \(\ell^1\) distance at most

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_k\left|\frac{r^{(m)}_{2k}}{\pi_{m,0}}
 -\frac{r^{(m)}_{2k+1}}{\pi_{m,1}}\right|
&\le\frac{\sum_k|r^{(m)}_{2k}-r^{(m)}_{2k+1}|
 +|\pi_{m,0}-\pi_{m,1}|}{\pi_{m,0}}\\
&\le16M_m.
\end{aligned}
\]

Let \(\nu_{m,b}\) be the law of \(Z_m\) conditional on \(X_m\equiv b\pmod2\). The aligned laws consequently have total variation at most \(8M_m\), and the alignment translates the rescaled odd law by only \(-M_m\). For every bounded Lipschitz function \(\varphi\), it follows that

\[
\left|\int\varphi\,d\nu_{m,0}-\int\varphi\,d\nu_{m,1}\right|
\le16M_m\|\varphi\|_\infty+M_m\operatorname{Lip}(\varphi)
\longrightarrow0.
\]

Since \(\nu_m=\pi_{m,0}\nu_{m,0}+\pi_{m,1}\nu_{m,1}\), each conditional law has the same weak limit \(\nu\). For completeness these conditional laws are tight, with tails at most four times the original tail bound because their conditioning masses are at least \(1/4\); bounded Lipschitz functions therefore determine their weak limits.

Under \(\Gamma_m\), the endpoints are independent given their common parity. Their rescaled joint law is exactly

\[
\sum_{b=0}^1\frac{\pi_{m,b}^2}{q(r^{(m)})}
       \nu_{m,b}\otimes\nu_{m,b}.
\]

Each product in this finite mixture converges weakly to \(\nu\otimes\nu\), and the mixture weights sum to one. Thus the joint law converges to \(\nu\otimes\nu\), and the continuous midpoint map shows that the rescaled midpoint law converges to the law of \((U_0+V_0)/2\) for independent \(U_0,V_0\) of law \(\nu\). On the other hand, the assumed Hellinger convergence gives \(\operatorname{TV}(r^{(m)},(r^{(m)})^{\mathrm{mid}})\to0\), and pushing both laws forward by the same scaling does not increase total variation. Their weak limits must therefore coincide. We obtain \(\nu=\mathcal L((U_0+V_0)/2)\). Its finite variance, already proved from the tail bounds, implies

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\nu)
=\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{U_0+V_0}{2}\right)
=\frac12\operatorname{Var}(\nu),
\]

contradicting strict positivity. This excludes \(M=0\) and completes the asserted one-dimensional compactness result.

To prove item 2, suppose that no positive absolute lower bound for \(d_{\mathrm H}^2(r,r^{\mathrm{mid}})/a(r)\), restricted to \(a(r)>0\), exists. Choose a sequence for which this ratio tends to zero. Because \(a(r)\le1\), its squared Hellinger distances tend to zero. By the compactness result, after translations and a subsequence it converges in \(\ell^1\) to a point mass or a uniform adjacent pair. Let \(I\) be that limiting support. Eventually \(r(I^c)\le1/1000\) and each endpoint of \(I\) has mass at least \(1/3\). The local estimate then bounds the same ratios below by \(1/16\), a contradiction. Their infimum is therefore positive. Choose a positive lower bound \(\kappa\le1\). Tables with \(a(r)=0\) satisfy the desired inequality automatically, proving item 2 for all the asserted tables. The compactness step is the only nonconstructive choice of a constant.

Finally consider a product as in item 3. For each factor apply the canonical definitions with \(p=r^{(i)}\), and put \(a_i=a(r^{(i)})\) and \(\eta_i=d_{\mathrm H}^2(r^{(i)},(r^{(i)})^{\mathrm{mid}})\). Before conditioning the coordinate pairs are independent, and equal parity is the intersection of their separate coordinatewise events. Conditioning therefore gives the product of the factor laws \(\Gamma_{r^{(i)}}\). It follows that \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}=\bigotimes_i(r^{(i)})^{\mathrm{mid}}\) and \(a(p)=1-\prod_i(1-a_i)\). Factoring Hellinger affinity gives \(d_{\mathrm H}^2(p,p^{\mathrm{mid}})=1-\prod_i(1-\eta_i)\). Since \(\eta_i\ge\kappa a_i\),

\[
d_{\mathrm H}^2(p,p^{\mathrm{mid}})
\ge1-\prod_i(1-\kappa a_i)
\ge\kappa\left(1-\prod_i(1-a_i)\right)
=\kappa a(p).
\]

For the second inequality, the polynomial \(F(t)=1-\prod_i(1-ta_i)\) has \(F(0)=0\) and is concave on \([0,1]\): differentiating twice gives \(F''(t)=-\sum_{i\ne j}a_i a_j\prod_{k\ne i,j}(1-ta_k)\le0\), with the sum empty when \(n=1\). Hence \(F(\kappa)\ge\kappa F(1)\). The previously proved comparison with total variation completes the product estimate.

Take the product of the one-dimensional global extensions constructed at the start of the proof, and denote this product extension by \(f\). It is finite-valued and agrees with the product table at every lattice tuple, including tuples with a zero factor. If its two endpoint values are positive, multiply the factorwise log-concavity inequalities; if an endpoint value is zero, the required inequality has right-hand side zero. This proves global log-concavity on all of \(\mathbb R^n\).

For \(T(x)=Ux+b_0\) as in the statement, \(T\) is a lattice bijection and \(U\) is invertible modulo two. Thus \(x\equiv y\pmod2\) if and only if \(T(x)\equiv T(y)\pmod2\), and \(T((x+y)/2)=(T(x)+T(y))/2\). The parity-conditioned joint law and midpoint law are consequently pushed forward by these bijections, while the diagonal event, Hellinger distance, and total variation are preserved. The transformed extension is \(f'(x)=f(U^{-1}(x-b_0))\), which is finite-valued and globally log-concave. Since \(U^{-1}\) has integer entries, its values at every lattice point are exactly those of the pushed-forward table, including every zero. This proves the remaining admissibility and invariance assertions.
statement:
Use the admissibility hypothesis and probability notation of accepted fact ab57fac07c0d3160. Explicitly, an admissible table in dimension \(n\ge1\) is a nonzero, nonnegative, finitely supported table \(w=(w_z)_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\) having a finite-valued globally log-concave extension \(f:\mathbb R^n\to[0,\infty)\) that agrees with \(w\) at every lattice point, including every zero. Global log-concavity means \(f((1-t)x+ty)\ge f(x)^{1-t}f(y)^t\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(0<t<1\), with a zero endpoint making the right-hand side zero. Set \(W=\sum_z w_z\), \(p_z=w_z/W\), \(A=\{z:p_z>0\}\), \(\pi_b=\sum_{z\equiv b\pmod2}p_z\), and \(q=\sum_b\pi_b^2\), where \(b\in(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^n\). Let \(\Gamma\) be the law of independent endpoints \(X,Y\) with table \(p\), conditioned on \(X\equiv Y\pmod2\), and let \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}\) be the law of \(J=(X+Y)/2\) under \(\Gamma\). Thus these are exactly the base-midpoint objects of that accepted fact. Write \(a(p)=\Gamma\{X\ne Y\}\).

For probability tables \(u,v\) on the same countable set, use \(\operatorname{TV}(u,v)=\frac12\sum_z|u_z-v_z|\) and define squared Hellinger distance by

\[
d_{\mathrm H}^2(u,v)
=\frac12\sum_z(\sqrt{u_z}-\sqrt{v_z})^2
=1-\sum_z\sqrt{u_zv_z}.
\]

The following statements hold.

1. In every dimension, \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}=p\) if and only if \(p\) is uniform on \(A\) and \(A\) contains at most one point of each parity class. In that case \(a(p)=0\). The assertion is within the admissible class; no parity-balance assumption or requirement that all parity classes be occupied is imposed.

2. There is an absolute constant \(\kappa\in(0,1]\) such that every finitely supported probability table \(r\) on \(\mathbb Z\) whose positive support is a nonempty integer interval and which satisfies \(r_k^2\ge r_{k-1}r_{k+1}\) for every \(k\in\mathbb Z\) obeys \(d_{\mathrm H}^2(r,r^{\mathrm{mid}})\ge\kappa a(r)\). Here \(r^{\mathrm{mid}},\pi_b(r),q(r),\Gamma_r,a(r)\) are the objects just defined with \(n=1\) and \(p=r\); this is an explicit specialization of the canonical notation, not a different midpoint operation.

3. For every \(n\ge1\) and every product \(p_z=\prod_{i=1}^n r^{(i)}_{z_i}\) of tables satisfying item 2,

   \[
   \kappa\,\Gamma\{X\ne Y\}
   \le d_{\mathrm H}^2(p,p^{\mathrm{mid}})
   \le\operatorname{TV}(p,p^{\mathrm{mid}}).
   \]

   Every such product is admissible, with an extension that agrees at all zero lattice values as well. For any \(U\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z)\) and \(b_0\in\mathbb Z^n\), its pushforward \(p'_{Uz+b_0}=p_z\) is also admissible and satisfies the same inequality with the same \(\kappa\). Thus \(\Gamma\{X\ne Y\}\le\kappa^{-1}\operatorname{TV}(p,p^{\mathrm{mid}})\) throughout this class.
